memory_leads.lead: Ship ownership and ship management are separable control layers. A registered or beneficial owner can retain asset ownership while delegating bounded technical, crewing, commercial or administrative functions to one or several managers; delegation changes who acts day to day without automatically changing title to the vessel.

Management scope is modular rather than one indivisible role. Technical management, crew management and commercial management may be bundled under one organization or split among different parties, so point-in-time replay should identify which function was actually delegated rather than infer authority from the generic label manager.

A management appointment creates a bounded mandate and reporting relationship. Appointment date, service commencement, delegated scope and later amendment or termination are distinct states from vessel ownership, bareboat control or commercial employment.

Owner-manager governance commonly requires an authority matrix: some routine technical, crewing and purchasing decisions may be delegated, while major unbudgeted expenditure, financing, sale, chartering strategy, major casualty decisions or structural modifications can remain reserved to the owner or require specific approval.

Technical budgets form a proposal-approval-execution-variance cycle. A manager can forecast maintenance, spares, stores, crew and repair expenditure, but owner approval and later variance review are separate from the underlying physical maintenance need; a budget is therefore not evidence that work was done.

Procurement authority has its own chain: onboard or superintendent requisition, manager review, budget or authority check, supplier selection, owner approval when required, purchase, expediting and receipt. Delegation can shorten routine purchasing while exceptional spend or conflicts can escalate back to the owner.

The superintendent or owner-representative interface is a governance bridge. Superintendents can inspect vessels, challenge priorities, coordinate yards and report technical status, while owner representatives may independently review manager recommendations; neither role should be collapsed into the onboard master or asset owner.

The master and onboard crew remain a distinct operational command layer even under third-party management. Shore management may supply procedures, personnel and resources, but immediate navigational and safety decisions aboard cannot be inferred solely from the commercial authority chain.

Management reporting is a recurring information pipeline: technical condition and defects, planned maintenance, incidents, crew status, purchasing, operating expenses, certificates or inspections and upcoming drydock work may reach the owner on different schedules and with different known times.

Owner instruction and manager recommendation are separate states. A manager may recommend repair, replacement, crew change, expenditure or operational restriction; the owner may approve, reject, defer or request alternatives where authority permits, so later execution should not overwrite the earlier recommendation or decision trail.

Management performance issues can move through observation, reporting, remediation request, escalation and review before any termination. Cost variance, repeated defects, crewing difficulty, weak reporting or incident response may trigger scrutiny, but a performance concern does not by itself prove contractual breach, negligence or legal liability.

Changing managers is an operational transition rather than a single contract date. Records, planned-maintenance history, open defects, spares, supplier orders, certificates, budgets, crew information, software/data access, yard plans and outstanding claims or invoices may require handover on different clocks.

Manager transition can temporarily increase operational risk even when the vessel continues trading because institutional knowledge, vendor relationships, system access and responsibility for open items must migrate. A new manager's service start therefore need not equal complete operational handover.

P057 maintenance memory is refined because maintenance due items, defects and spares queues are acted on through a governance layer: the technically preferred action can be delayed, accelerated or altered by delegated authority, owner approvals, budget controls and reporting cadence.

P046 vessel-identity memory is refined because beneficial owner, registered owner, bareboat charterer/operator and technical or crew manager can coexist around one hull. Operational control must therefore be represented role-by-role rather than inferred from a single company name.

P052 port-call memory is refined because the party arranging agents, husbandry, crew logistics or technical attendance may be a delegated manager acting for the owner/operator; appointment authority and ultimate economic or legal responsibility should remain separate.

P054 casualty memory is refined because casualty response can involve master, owner, technical manager, insurer/P&I and authorities on overlapping authority chains; identifying who coordinated an action should not be treated as automatic proof of fault or ultimate liability.

Earlier Shipping passes already distinguish owner, operator, technical manager, superintendent and onboard roles. P058 adds the delegated-governance and transition state machine rather than rediscovering those actor labels.

P057 already maps maintenance budgeting, procurement and service dependencies. P058 reuses those operational queues to describe owner-manager authorization and oversight without creating a second maintenance semantic owner.

stop_reason: The delegated ship-management governance layer is populated from functional scope and appointment through authority matrices, budget/procurement approval, superintendent and master interfaces, recurring reporting, recommendation/instruction trails, performance escalation and manager transition/handover. Further recall becomes agreement-, fee-, authority-limit-, KPI-, liability-, provider- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation and not legal, management, crewing, technical, procurement or investment advice; no management agreement, delegated authority, fee, budget threshold, procurement term, KPI, breach, liability, provider capability, owner instruction or manager-transition fact is verified.
